newsitem.title: USA: Agronomist lowers Kansas wheat damage estimate.
newsitem.headline: Agronomist lowers Kansas wheat damage estimate.

text.p: Shriveled and dead wheat plants in Kansas and Oklahoma have crop experts expecting severe losses, but one Kansas agronomist expressed a little more optimism for the crop than he had last week.
"I was really discouraged on Wednesday, but I'm a little more optimistic now," said Rollie Sears, a wheat breeder at Kansas State University touring south central Kansas Saturday.
He said a second survey this past Saturday of wheat fields indicated losses in Kansas may be closer to 100 million bushels, rather than the 100 million to 150 million estimated last week.
However, he said plants that survive would yield low-protein and low test-weight grain and produce poor flour.
"If we don't get too much disease and relatively good weather maybe this stem damage will be minimized," he said."

Agricultural statistics services for the respective states rated wheat in Kansas as of Sunday 60 percent very poor to fair versus 37 percent the previous week, Oklahoma 58 percent very poor to fair versus 34 the previous week and Texas 68 percent very poor to fair versus 39 the previous week.

Crop experts in Kansas and Oklahoma said it will be at least another week before accurate damage assessments can be made. By that time most of the freeze-hit wheat plants will have wilted or turned black. However, the hardest hit wheat in southwest Kansas and the Oklahoma Panhandle has already wilted or died.
"I thought we had a good shot at a 400-million-bushel crop and I think realistically we are looking somewhere around 300 million now," said Sears of the Kansas crop.

Sears said Saturday's tour found wheat in eastern sections of Cowley, Sedgwick and Sumner Counties in south central Kansas in better condition than the freeze-damaged wheat in western areas of the counties. South central and southwest Kansas produce about a quarter of Kansas' wheat.
In the Oklahoma Panhandle, crop damage ranged up to 100 percent, said Tom Stephens, chairman of the Oklahoma Wheat Commission, and a Guymon, Okla., wheat farmer.
In many fields, he said, wheat plants would be putting out secondary tillers which would delay harvest up to 30 days.
"We are still assessing it. But, we've looked at some fields with 50 to 100 percent damage," he said.

An Oklahoma State University agronomist said the hardest hit plants were west of Interstate Highway 35, which runs north-south and bisects the state through Oklahoma City. In some sections of southwest Oklahoma, where the wheat was headed or about to head, losses may be as high as 75 percent, said Kim Anderson, Oklahoma State University agronomist.
Prior to the freeze, some Oklahoma grain merchants estimated the wheat crop at 182 million bushels, versus last year's dry-weather-hit crop of 93.1 million.
